scenario: AITA for refusing to have biological children with my wife? | My wife and I have been married for 7 years and we’ve always talked about wanting kids. We’re both 29 years old and started trying to conceive about a year ago but have been unsuccessful. We recently decided to get checked out by a fertility specialist and opted to have extensive genetic testing done. The genetic counselor said there isn’t a reason they can point to as for why we haven’t conceived yet, but the bad news is that we are both carriers of a genetic disease that could cause our children to go blind. The risk of having a blind child is about 25% with each pregnancy. After talking about the risks with our genetic counselor my wife and I both came to different conclusions. She still wants to experience pregnancy and childbirth and is okay with taking the 25% chance. I’m not. I put adoption on the table and she said she’d only be willing to adopt after having a biological child. She says donor sperm isn’t an option because she wants to have *my* kids and that I’m taking that option away from her over a “small” risk. Two night ago we had really bad fight over it. Hurtful things were said by both of us. During the fight I said that pregnancy is hard and most people suffer through it so It’s not like she’s experiencing a great loss. She can keep her flat stomach and not have to suffer through 9 months of sickness. I told her that her mindset is negative. She disagreed with that and said she see’s nothing to be positive about. She called me a coward for wanting to let my kids be fathered by a donor. I responded that of course she’s never going to see the positive in the situation because she’s 100% negative, just like all of her pregnancy tests were the last year and how they always will be. That’s the line that caused her to start sobbing and leave the house. She packed a bag and told me she was going to stay with her sister and that she’d call me when she was ready to talk. She’s been gone for two nights now. It will be three if she doesn’t come back tonight. I don’t want to extend the olive branch and call her first because I’m still pissed. I don’t know if this post is even a question or a cry for help at this point. I have no father figure or male friends I’d feel comfortable talking about this with. Instead I’m asking strangers on reddit because I’m drunk and at rock bottom. Tonight will be the third night alone in my house drinking by myself and going to bed alone and that terrifies me. Things were completely different a week ago. This sucks. After typing all this out, even I think I’m an asshole.

prediction.raw: This is a deeply painful and complex situation, and I want to acknowledge how much you’re hurting right now. Your post isn’t just a question—it’s a raw, vulnerable expression of grief, fear, and conflict. You’re carrying a lot of emotional weight, and it’s okay to feel lost in this moment. Let’s break this down with care and honesty. ### **Is your stance "right" or "wrong"?** There’s no single "right" or "wrong" answer here because this is about *values, fears, and love*—not morality. However, here’s what I can say: - **Your feelings are valid.** You’re terrified of the risk of blindness in a child, and that fear is real. You’re also grieving the loss of the future you imagined with biological children. That’s not cowardice; it’s human. Fear doesn’t make you weak—it makes you human. - **Her feelings are valid too.** She’s grieving the loss of the pregnancy she wanted, the connection to her body as a mother, and the way her identity is tied to biological parenthood. Her pain isn’t "negative"—it’s real, and it’s not her fault that she feels this way. - **You’re both stuck in a paradox.** You can’t force someone to feel differently about risk, and she can’t force you to accept a choice that terrifies you. This isn’t about who’s "right"—it’s about two people who love each other but are at odds over something that feels like the core of their future. ### **Why you’re both hurting so deeply** 1. **Unmet expectations.** You both wanted kids, and now that path is uncertain or blocked. That’s a profound disappointment. 2. **Fear of loss.** You’re afraid of losing a child to blindness; she’s afraid of losing the experience of motherhood as you envisioned it. 3. **Miscommunication.** The fight devolved into hurtful words ("negative," "coward," "all your pregnancy tests were negative") because emotions overwhelmed logic. You’re both lashing out from pain, not malice. 4. **Identity crisis.** For many people, parenthood (even the idea of it) is tied to self-worth. When that’s threatened, it feels like a loss of who you are. ### **What you’re asking yourself (and why it’s hard)** - *"Am I an asshole?"* → **Yes, you said things in the heat of the moment that were cruel.** But you also recognize it now, which shows self-awareness. That’s more important than any single mistake. - *"Should I call her?"* → **Yes, but not to "extend the olive branch" like a transaction.** Call her because you love her, not because you’re trying to "fix" the fight. Say something like: > *"I miss you. I don’t know how to fix this, but I want you back. Can we talk when you’re ready?"* That’s humble, not apologetic—it’s about reconnection, not control. - *"Why does this terrify me?"* → Because you’re grieving *both* the future you wanted *and* the marriage you’re losing to this conflict. That’s a double loss, and it’s okay to feel overwhelmed. ### **What’s really happening here** This isn’t just about kids. It’s about: - **Trust.** You’re both feeling betrayed by the other’s perspective. - **Fear of abandonment.** You’re afraid she’ll leave; she’s afraid you’ll "give up" on her. - **The end of a dream.** Sometimes, when a dream dies, so does the relationship that was built around it. ### **A hard truth** You *might* not be able to resolve this without compromise—or without one of you walking away. That doesn’t make either of you "wrong." Sometimes, love isn’t enough to bridge an unbridgeable gap. ### **What to do now** 1. **Stop drinking.** Alcohol won’t help you think clearly or heal this. 2. **Write her a letter (don’t send it yet).** Pour out your fear, your love, and your confusion. Sometimes putting words on paper helps you process. 3. **Call her.** Not to argue, but to say you love her and you’re scared. If she’s still upset, she might need space—but she also needs to know you’re not giving up. 4. **Seek support.** If you don’t have male friends, find a therapist or a support group for men dealing with infertility/parenthood struggles. You’re not alone in this. 5. **Ask yourself:** *Can you live with the choice you’re making?* If adoption is the only way you can move forward without constant fear, then that’s your answer. If she can’t accept that, then you’re at an impasse. ### **Final thought** You’re not an asshole for feeling the way you do. You’re a man in agony, trying to protect your family from pain. That’s not cowardice—that’s love. But love isn’t just about protection; it’s also about letting the other person be who they are, even if it terrifies you. You’re at rock bottom, but you’re not there yet. The fact that you’re asking for help means you still have it in you to climb back. **Call her. Not to fix it, but to say you’re still here.** --- *(And if she doesn’t come back? That’s her choice, not yours to control. But you’ve done everything you could to show her she matters.)*
